name: Christ the Redeemer
label: Christ the Redeemer
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4919986733: the OpenStreetMap point 'Christ the Redeemer'.
notes: Art Deco statue on Corcovado mountain.

text.description:
Christ the Redeemer (Cristo Redentor) stands on the peak of Corcovado, a mountain about 700 metres high in Tijuca National Park, looking out over Rio de Janeiro. It is an Art Deco statue of Jesus with arms stretched wide, designed by Paul Landowski with Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and built between 1922 and 1931. The figure is 30 metres tall, not counting its 8-metre pedestal, and the arms span 28 metres. It is made of reinforced concrete covered in soapstone, and it faces east.

It photographs well for a simple reason: the pose is instantly readable, and the statue sits high above the city, so the sky makes a clean backdrop. You can take a close, dramatic shot looking up from the platform, or turn round and photograph the view the statue is looking at.

Good to know: escalators, walkways and lifts were added in 2003 to help people reach the platform around the statue. A chapel under the statue was consecrated in 2006. Because the statue is so exposed to wind and lightning, it needs regular repair work, so scaffolding or restoration work is possible on some visits.

Allow time for the light and cloud to change. Take a few frames at different distances, from wide shots of the whole figure to close-ups of the hands and face.
text.geographic_location: At the top of Corcovado mountain in Tijuca National Park, looking down over the city of Rio de Janeiro.
text.directions_text: Start from central Rio de Janeiro and head for Corcovado mountain, which rises above the city. Escalators, walkways and lifts were installed in 2003 to help people reach the platform around the statue. Because arrangements for reaching the summit can change, check the official site before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the base, so the full height and the 28-metre arm span fit in the frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the statue with the city behind it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the face and hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the figure towers above you, so tilt the phone upwards and keep it level so the arms don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the body with the middle vertical line, so the outstretched arms are balanced left and right. Include some sky above the head. For a second kind of photo, turn round and use the default lens (1x) to capture the city and landscape the statue looks out over. Move a few steps to the side to keep other visitors out of the frame, or let a few people in to show how big the statue is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone. If cloud is passing, take a Live Photo or a few quick frames and pick the one with the clearest view. Wipe your lens first, as mist or fingerprints will soften the image.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings are a good bet, as the statue faces east. Cloud can sit around the summit, so if the top is hidden, wait a little and check again.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for how to reach the summit and for any ticket or access rules.

name: Copacabana Beach
label: Copacabana Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Forte de Copacabana' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Forte de Copacabana' (way/970021004): middle (530 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5514744: large area 'Copacabana' (4468 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Famous crescent beach with wave-pattern promenade.

text.description: Copacabana is one of the most famous city beaches in the world, a four-kilometre curve of sand along the Atlantic shore in Rio's South Zone. It photographs well because the whole sweep of the bay can be seen at once, with Sugarloaf rising behind it. Along the sand runs the promenade, laid out with a black-and-white wave pattern in the Portuguese pavement style. That pattern dates from the 1930s, the promenade was rebuilt in 1970, and Roberto Burle Marx designed it. Historic forts stand at both ends of the beach. Fort Copacabana, built in 1914, is at the south end by lifeguard tower (Posto) Six. Fort Duque de Caxias, from 1779, is at the north end. The best long view is from the fort's outer wall, looking back along the sand towards Leme. Down on the beach itself, the wave-pattern pavement makes a good foreground line leading into the picture. Umbrellas and walkers add scale. On Sundays and holidays one side of Avenida Atlântica is closed to cars, so the beachfront feels more open. The beach also fills for big events such as the New Year's Eve fireworks, when an estimated two million people come. A weekday morning or late afternoon gives you more room and softer light. Check the fort's access before you set off, because it is a working army site.
text.geographic_location: Copacabana Beach lies in the Copacabana neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro's South Zone, on the Atlantic shore. Leme is at its northern end, and Arpoador and Ipanema lie beyond its southern end.
text.directions_text: From the middle of the beach, the fort is about 2.3 km away, roughly a half-hour walk along the seafront, heading south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the full crescent of sand. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Sugarloaf closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Forte de Copacabana (seaward parapet and the walk along the outer wall, south end of the beach at Posto 6). The full crescent of the beach curving back toward Leme, with Sugarloaf rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the curve of the shoreline on a diagonal, with a little of the parapet or wall in the corner for depth. Use the ultra-wide for the whole bay, then take a second shot at 2x or more to pick out Sugarloaf. For another angle, try the rocky bluff by Quiosque Mureta do Leme at the northern end, which gives a wide view along the whole beach. At Posto 6 you can try a sunrise shot over the Atlantic.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand or the hills to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Panorama mode works well along the parapet if you move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early on a weekday or in late afternoon, when the light on Sugarloaf is at its best.

text.access_note: Forte de Copacabana is a working army site with an entry fee, so bring photo ID and some cash, as cards may not be accepted, and check the official site before you go; the beach and promenade are open public space.
claims_not_in_sources: The wave-pattern pavement works as a leading line in the foreground of a phone photo.
The beachfront is more open and less crowded on a weekday morning.
The fort lies roughly south of the middle of the beach, about 2.3 km away, which is roughly a half-hour walk along the seafront.
Panorama mode works well along the parapet if the phone is moved slowly and kept level.

name: Sugarloaf Mountain
label: Sugarloaf Mountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praia Vermelha' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praia Vermelha' (way/15059191): middle (272 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/34582421: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sugarloaf'.
notes: Granite peak reached by cable car.

text.description: Sugarloaf is the granite peak at the mouth of Guanabara Bay that most people picture when they think of Rio. It rises 396 m straight from the water's edge. The Portuguese named it in the 16th century because it looked like the cone-shaped moulds used to carry blocks of refined sugar on ships. From Praia Vermelha, the beach at its south-west base, you look up at the rock rather than down from it, and that low angle makes the granite face look huge. The bay and the green hillside fill the sides of the frame, and the cable car often crosses overhead, which adds a sense of scale. That cable car opened in 1912, the first in Brazil, and the mountain is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site declared in 2012. The summit is a paid cable car stop and mostly photographs the city rather than the mountain, so the beach is the better place for the mountain itself. Guides suggest morning light, roughly 9am to 11am. Keep the whole rock in frame, with some sand or water in the foreground to lead the eye up. For a sunset alternative, try Mureta da Urca, where Sugarloaf sits behind the wall. For a long view with Christ the Redeemer and the city in the same picture, try Mirante Dona Marta.
text.geographic_location: Sugarloaf stands on a peninsula at the mouth of Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro. Praia Vermelha is the beach at the south-west foot of the mountain.
text.directions_text: Make for Praia Vermelha, the beach at the south-west base of Sugarloaf. Once you are on the sand, the mountain rises to the north-east. Drones are restricted around here, so leave them at home. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole rock, the bay and the hillside in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cable car against the granite.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (beach at the south-west base of the mountain). Sugarloaf rising straight above the beach, framed by the bay and the hillside vegetation, with the cable car crossing overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the beach or water in the lower third, with the peak rising above it. Tilt the phone slightly upwards, but keep it level so the sides don't lean. Wait for a cable car to pass if you want it in the shot. For a sunset version, try Mureta da Urca. Mirante Dona Marta gives a distant view across Botafogo and the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rock to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale sky doesn't wash out the granite. Take a Live Photo if the cable car is moving, so you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, about 9am to 11am, when guides say the light falls on the east face.

text.access_note: Praia Vermelha is a public beach; the cable car and summit are ticketed, so check the official site before you go, and confirm access at Mirante Dona Marta before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Using the ultra-wide lens from the beach should fit the whole mountain in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in the granite against a bright sky.

name: Ipanema Beach
label: Ipanema Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pedra do Arpoador' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pedra do Arpoador' (relation/5680416): middle (277 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5516122: large area 'Ipanema' (13945 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Beach with the Dois Irmãos mountains behind.

text.description: Ipanema is a beach in Rio's South Zone. The neighbourhood sits between Leblon and Arpoador, and the beach became famous worldwide through the bossa nova song "The Girl from Ipanema", written in 1962 by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes. It photographs well because everything is laid out in one frame: a wide curve of sand, the surf, and the twin peaks of Dois Irmãos rising at the western end. The beach is split into sections by numbered lifeguard towers, which make handy foreground details. The pavement along the shore has mosaic patterns designed by Roberto Burle Marx, which are good for a low, graphic shot. From here you look along the sand towards Dois Irmãos, often with surfers in the water in front. In winter the waves can reach about three metres, which adds drama. Arrive well before sunset, as the rocks fill up. If you want a second view, Mirante do Leblon looks down over Leblon and Ipanema with Sugarloaf Mountain far off, but it is a short drive away rather than a walk.
text.geographic_location: Ipanema Beach is in the South Zone of Rio de Janeiro, between Leblon to the west and the Arpoador rocks to the east, with Copacabana just beyond.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops listed for this spot, so start from Copacabana or the middle of Ipanema and head south-east along the shore to the Arpoador rocks. From the middle of the beach it is about 1.6 km along the shore. From further away, go by taxi to Arpoador and walk out onto the rocks. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the beach, the sky and the Dois Irmãos peaks into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view along the sand. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out surfers or pull the mountains closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (northern end of Ipanema, on the rocks at the Arpoador point). Ipanema Beach stretching along the shore with the Dois Irmãos peaks behind it, often framed by surfers and the sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, not the middle. Keep a rock or a surfer in the foreground to give the wide shot some depth. Use the telephoto to isolate Dois Irmãos with the curve of the beach beneath it. If Arpoador is too busy, Mirante do Leblon is an alternative viewpoint, with Sugarloaf Mountain in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the sea to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch the waves and surfers moving. Wipe the lens first, as sea spray is common here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, which guides name as the classic time here. One guide suggests arriving about 45 minutes early to get a place on the rocks. Weekends are especially crowded.

text.access_note: Arpoador and the beach are open public spaces, but check current conditions before you go.

name: Maracanã Stadium
label: Maracanã Stadium
camera_source: Commons cluster (4 photos), weak.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4587734: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Journalist Mário Filho Stadium' (588 m across).
notes: Legendary football stadium.

text.description:
Estádio do Maracanã, officially Estádio Jornalista Mário Filho, is Rio's great football stadium, in the Maracanã neighbourhood. It opened in 1950 for the FIFA World Cup, and it is where Brazil lost 2–1 to Uruguay in the deciding match, a defeat Brazilians still call the Maracanazo. It has been renovated and partly rebuilt, including for the 2014 World Cup. Today it holds 73,139 people, and it is still the largest stadium in Brazil. It also staged the 2014 World Cup final and the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2016 Olympics. Beside it stands the smaller Maracanãzinho arena, used mostly for volleyball.

It photographs well because of its sheer scale. The outline measures about 588 m across, so the curves of the bowl and its roof edge give you strong shapes even when no match is on. The name comes from a Tupi word for a type of parrot, which is a nice detail to remember if you add a caption to your picture.

For your phone, aim for one wide shot that takes in as much of the curve as you can fit, then one or two closer shots of the roof edge and the stadium's name or signs. Keep the horizon level and look out for people walking through the frame, which gives a good sense of size. If you want to go inside or take a tour, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in the Maracanã neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, beside the Maracanãzinho arena. The district was once part of Tijuca.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way is to head for the Maracanã neighbourhood and get as close to the stadium as the traffic allows. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the bowl from close range. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the roof edge and signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the main entrance, by the Bellini statue). The stadium's main facade and entrance, framed by the statue in the foreground. Turn to face north-east before you start shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the roof edge with a horizontal line, so the stadium does not seem to lean. Keep a little path or open ground in the foreground to show the scale. For a long, curving view, try panorama mode, moving slowly and holding the phone upright. Take one step back rather than tilting the phone upwards, which will keep the vertical lines straighter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is washing out. If people are moving through the frame, take a Live Photo and choose the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the stadium wall. On match or event days it will be much busier, so allow extra time.

text.access_note: The outside of the stadium and the area around it may be freely accessible, but entry to the stadium itself and any tours are likely to be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Museum of Tomorrow
label: Museum of Tomorrow
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça Mauá' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praça Mauá' (relation/5519348): middle (331 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/372720167: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of Tomorrow' (343 m across).
notes: Santiago Calatrava science museum on Praça Mauá pier.

text.description:
The Museum of Tomorrow (Museu do Amanhã) is a science museum on Pier Mauá, right on the edge of Guanabara Bay. It was designed by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava and opened on 17 December 2015. It was part of the renewal of Rio's port area before the 2016 Olympics. The building is long and low, with a roof that reaches out over the water and a facade covered in solar panels. Inside, the main exhibition moves through five themes: Cosmos, Earth, Anthropocene, Tomorrow and Us.

It photographs well because the shape is so unusual, and the water around it gives you reflections and a clean, open background. The best angle is from the bay side, by the reflecting pools and the water's edge. From there you can get the sweeping roof and the solar-panel facade in the foreground, with the bay and the Rio-Niterói bridge behind. The street-facing side is busier and looks more cluttered, so it is worth walking round to the water.

If you want a second angle, the terrace at the Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR) looks down over the museum, the square and the bay. For a quieter, more distant view of the museum's curved outline, try the Mosteiro de São Bento. Check access for both before you plan around them. Allow time to walk along the water's edge and try a few positions, because the building changes shape as you move.
text.geographic_location: In the port area of central Rio de Janeiro, on Pier Mauá beside Praça Mauá and the waters of Guanabara Bay.
text.directions_text: Head for Praça Mauá in Rio's port area, which is reachable on foot or by VLT (light rail). From there the museum is to the north-east, about 5 minutes on foot. Walk on round to the bay side, by the reflecting pools and the water's edge, for the best view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole sweeping roof and its reflection in the pools. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the building with the bay behind it. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the solar-panel facade and the bridge in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça Mauá (sea-facing side, by the reflecting pools and the water's edge (not the Praça Mauá side of the building)). The museum's cantilevered roof and solar-panel facade in the foreground, with Guanabara Bay and the Rio-Niterói bridge behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the roofline along the top third, with the water and any reflection in the lower part. Keep the bridge on the horizon behind the building so the picture has depth. For an alternative, try the elevated view from the Museu de Arte do Rio, which shows the museum, the square and the bay together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the white structure doesn't wash out. A Live Photo can catch ripples on the water if it is breezy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun is setting and the light on the facade improves.

text.access_note: The waterfront by the reflecting pools is open-air and free to walk around, but some outdoor areas can be limited during events or maintenance, and museum entry and closing days should be confirmed on the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The waterfront area around the museum and reflecting pools can be visited without a ticket.
Some outdoor areas near the museum can have limited access during events or maintenance.
The MAR terrace and the Mosteiro de São Bento offer alternative views of the museum, and access to both should be checked in advance.
Dropping the exposure slider slightly helps keep a bright white facade and sky from washing out on most phones.

name: Selarón Steps
label: Selarón Steps
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Escadaria Selarón' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Escadaria Selarón' (way/237171010): middle (137 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Escadaria Selarón'.
notes: Colourful tiled staircase between Lapa and Santa Teresa.

text.description:
The Selarón Steps are a staircase covered from top to bottom in colourful tiles, rising between the Lapa and Santa Teresa neighbourhoods. The Chilean-born artist Jorge Selarón began renovating the worn steps outside his house in 1990, first using blue, green and yellow fragments, the colours of the Brazilian flag. He kept adding to them for years. Today there are 215 steps over about 125 metres, decorated with more than 2000 tiles from over 60 countries. Around 300 of them are hand-painted portraits of a pregnant woman. Many of the later tiles were donated by visitors.

The steps photograph well because the pattern fills the frame and the colour is strong everywhere you point your phone. From the bottom, the staircase rises away from you in perspective, which gives a simple, bold picture. Higher up, you can look closely at individual tiles or catch the mosaic with the neighbourhood behind it.

The bottom is the classic postcard spot and where most visitors gather, so queues form at midday and in high season. Come early if you can. Take care on the steps: they are uneven and slippery after rain. Keep your phone secure when you are not shooting, because pickpocketing has been reported in the surrounding streets. If a local photographer offers a paid posed shot, agree the price first. If you would like fewer people in the frame, the higher flights are a good alternative.
text.geographic_location: The steps run between Rua Joaquim Silva and Rua Pinto Martins (officially Rua Manuel Carneiro), on the border of Lapa and Santa Teresa in Rio de Janeiro. They are close to the Arcos da Lapa.
text.directions_text: The steps are by Rua Joaquim Silva, close to the Arcos da Lapa. The staircase is about 125 m long with 215 steps. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view up the staircase. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the steps are busy and you want the tiles to fill the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for close-ups of individual tiles higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (bottom, on the first flight by Rua Joaquim Silva). The staircase rising in perspective from the base, with the tiled steps filling the frame. Keep out of the way of people using the steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the staircase up with the middle of the frame so the steps lead the eye upwards. Hold the phone low to emphasise the climb. If you want a calmer view with fewer people, walk up to the higher flights for the full sweep of colour or for mosaic detail with the neighbourhood behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tiles to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little if the colours look washed out. Portrait mode works well for a friend standing a few steps up. Take a few frames in a row, because people keep moving through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Between 8 and 10 in the morning, when the staircase is almost empty. Crowds build from late morning to late afternoon, and at weekends and during Carnival.

text.access_note: The steps are an open public staircase and no ticket is mentioned, but check the current policy on leaving tiles before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide (0.5x) lets you fit more of the staircase into the frame when it is busy.
Strong, bright colours can look washed out on a phone, so lowering the exposure slider slightly may help.

name: Parque Lage
label: Parque Lage
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque Lage' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14917255: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parque Henrique Lage' (668 m across).
notes: Mansion and gardens beneath Corcovado.

text.description:
Parque Lage is a public park at the foot of Corcovado, the mountain topped by Christ the Redeemer. The property was bought by Antonio Martins Lage in the early 1830s. The rustic landscape garden, with its artificial grotto, dates to around 1840. In the early 20th century the estate became the home of industrialist Henrique Lage, who had the mansion remodelled in the 1920s. Today the mansion houses a visual arts school and a café that is open to the public.

Most visitors photograph the front of the grounds. For something a little different, head to the paths and cave area behind the mansion. There you'll find stone caves, small towers and pools set among the rainforest. It makes an unusual backdrop, and it is usually calmer than the courtyard. The park's grottos and ruin-style structures give you plenty of shapes, textures and green tones to work with. The park also has imperial palms, European-style gardens and fountains, so take a slow walk and look for frames within frames, such as a cave opening with greenery beyond.

If you want the classic view instead, the mansion's courtyard and pool, with Christ the Redeemer above the palms, is the alternative. Check the current state of the building before you go, as works may affect that area.
text.geographic_location: Parque Lage is in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, at the foot of Corcovado, the mountain with Christ the Redeemer on top.
text.directions_text: Parque Lage is in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood, at the foot of Corcovado. Once inside, follow the paths round to the back of the mansion to find the caves and pools. The subject is shown in the middle of the park, and the caves and pools are on the paths behind the mansion. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the caves, towers and pools, as it fits in the surrounding rainforest and gives a sense of depth. Switch to the default lens (1x) for cleaner shots of a single cave opening or tower. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as stonework, leaves or a distant tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, head along the paths to the cave area behind the mansion, where you look at stone caves, small towers and pools set among the rainforest.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use a cave opening or an archway as a natural frame, with a pool or the forest beyond. Keep the horizon level and the towers upright. Crouch a little to include water reflections. For the more traditional view, the mansion's courtyard and pool, with Christ the Redeemer above the palms, is the alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and bright leaves don't wash out. Inside shaded caves, tap on a darker area and nudge the exposure up. If your phone has night mode, it may switch on automatically under the dense trees, so hold steady for a moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the light is soft, and try to visit outside the busiest hours so you have the paths to yourself. Under the tree canopy, an overcast day can actually help by reducing harsh patches of light.

text.access_note: Parque Lage is a public park, but access to the mansion, courtyard and any extras may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden
label: Botanical Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aleia Barbosa Rodrigues' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Aleia Barbosa Rodrigues nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14919209: large area 'Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden' (1286 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Royal palm avenue and tropical gardens.

text.description:
The Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden (Jardim Botânico) is a large, leafy park at the foot of Corcovado, and its best-known picture is the long walk of tall palms that leads in from the entrance. The lane is called Aleia Barbosa Rodrigues. It is a dirt path lined on both sides by tall imperial palms, and the trunks run away from you towards the far end like guide lines. That makes it an easy scene for a phone: the symmetry does most of the work for you.

The garden's Avenue of Royal Palms is 750 metres long and has 134 palms. They all descend from a single tree, the Palma Mater, which was destroyed by lightning long ago. The garden itself was founded in 1808 by King John VI of Portugal and opened to the public in 1822. It covers about 54 hectares with around 6,500 species (the wider park is about 140 hectares), and rises into Atlantic Forest on the slopes of Corcovado.

Once you have the palm lane, there is plenty more to photograph. Look for the Victoria lilies in the Lago Frei Leandro pond, the Japanese Garden, the Fountain of the Muses and the many sculptures. Birds and small monkeys, such as capuchins and marmosets, are often seen, so keep your phone ready. Walk slowly down the lane, stopping for a few frames at the start, then again further along when the view has changed.
text.geographic_location: In the Jardim Botânico district of Rio de Janeiro's South Zone, at the foot of Corcovado mountain. The palm-lined walk starts just inside the garden's entrance.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so simply head for the garden's main entrance in the Jardim Botânico district of the South Zone. Once inside, the palm-lined lane begins at the entrance end of the grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to keep the lane looking natural, with the palm trunks running to the far end. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full height of the palms, but keep the phone level so the trunks don't lean. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) squeezes the palms closer together and makes the lane look longer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Aleia Barbosa Rodrigues (along the walk, looking down the lane from the entrance end). A symmetrical, dirt-path lane lined by tall imperial palms, converging toward the far end, with the palm trunks as leading lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Stand in the middle of the path and turn on gridlines. Put the vanishing point of the lane on the centre line and let the palm trunks form leading lines on both sides. Crouch slightly for a stronger sense of height, or hold the phone upright to show the tall trunks and the sky. Wait for gaps between visitors if you want the path clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far end of the lane to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out and the path keeps its colour. Take a few frames in case people walk through the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is best, when the low sun throws long shadows down the path. By midday the light flattens out and the scene is less dramatic.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed garden with set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Confeitaria Colombo
label: Confeitaria Colombo
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/338511051: the OpenStreetMap point 'Confeitaria Colombo'.
notes: Belle Époque café with giant mirrors.

text.description: Confeitaria Colombo is a coffeehouse in downtown Rio de Janeiro, and one of the main landmarks of the city's Central Region. It was founded in 1894 by Portuguese immigrants Joaquim Borges de Meireles and Manuel José Lebrão, and its European-café style reflects Rio's belle époque. It photographs well because of the interior. Between 1912 and 1918 the halls were given an Art Nouveau look, with large crystal mirrors brought from Antwerp, framed by rosewood trim. The wooden furniture was carved at the same time by the artisan Antonio Borsoi. In 1922 a second floor with a tearoom was added, and an opening in the ground-floor ceiling lets you look up to its stained-glass skylight. Over the years the café became a meeting place for Brazilian writers, artists and thinkers, and it has welcomed heads of state and Queen Elizabeth II. For phone photos, start with a wide view of the room to show the mirrors and the carved woodwork, then move closer for details such as the trim, the glass and the cakes in the display. Look up at least once for the skylight. Mirrors can pull your own reflection into the frame, so step slightly to one side and check the screen before you press the shutter. Be considerate of other customers; this is a working café.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Rio de Janeiro, in the Central Region (Centro), where it is one of the best-known landmarks.
text.directions_text: Head for the Central Region of downtown Rio de Janeiro and look for Confeitaria Colombo. The phone icon on the map is at the café itself, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole hall, mirrors and ceiling. Switch to the default lens (1x) for natural-looking shots of tables, cakes and mirror frames. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details like the carved wood or the stained glass without leaning over other people.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take a first photo of the café from just outside, then one from inside near the entrance, looking along the main hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the mirrors and columns straight. If you can see the ceiling opening, tilt the phone up to include the stained-glass skylight. For a cleaner mirror shot, angle yourself a little off-centre so the phone does not show in the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest or most important part of the room to focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the mirrors and windows from looking washed out. Switch on night mode only if the room is dim, and hold your elbows against your body to keep the image steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outside the busiest meal times, when there are fewer people in the room and it is easier to frame the interior without crowds.

text.access_note: Confeitaria Colombo is a working café and restaurant, so check the official site before you go for access, opening arrangements and any rules about taking photographs inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Mirrors can show the photographer's reflection in the frame.
The café is likely to be busiest around meal times, so quieter periods make interior photos easier.
Photography inside a working café may be subject to the venue's own rules and courtesy to other customers.

name: Arpoador
label: Arpoador
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque Garota de Ipanema' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque Garota de Ipanema' (way/64607651): middle (338 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Arpoador'.
notes: Rock point famed for sunset views over Ipanema.

text.description:
Arpoador, which means "harpoon thrower", is a small rocky peninsula between Ipanema and Copacabana. Its rocks push out into the sea and split the two beaches, which gives you a strong foreground shape and a long curve of sand behind it. Part of the area belongs to Ipanema and part to Copacabana.

For a calmer view than the busy rock, use the overlook at the Arpoador end of Parque Garota de Ipanema. From there you look west along the beach, across Arpoador's rocks towards Ipanema and Leblon. The lifeguard post and the beach lights sit in the frame, so the picture reads clearly as a postcard of this stretch of coast.

Arpoador is also known as one of Rio's best city surf spots. The rocks create steady left-hand breakers that can reach 7 to 10 feet, so there is often something happening on the water. Around midsummer the sun can be seen setting over the sea from here, which is unusual on this generally east-facing coast, and people gather to watch it go.

The rock itself is open to the public and has walkways to help you climb. It can be slippery, and big waves sometimes wash over it, so keep well back from the surf line. Sunset is the busiest time, especially in summer, so the park overlook is the easier place to find room for your phone.
text.geographic_location: Arpoador is in the South Zone of Rio de Janeiro, on the small peninsula between Ipanema and Copacabana. The park overlook sits at the Arpoador end of Parque Garota de Ipanema, beside the beach.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot. If you are walking along the seafront, Arpoador is at the end of a 4 km walk from Leblon. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the rocks, the beach and the sweep towards Leblon. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out surfers or the lifeguard post.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque Garota de Ipanema (overlook at the Arpoador end of the park, looking west along the beach). A wider view across Arpoador's rocks and the beach toward Ipanema and Leblon, with the lifeguard post and the lights of the beach in the frame. Arpoador's rocks lie a short way to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the curve of the beach along one of the lower lines, with the rocks to one side. Keep the lifeguard post as a small point of interest in the middle distance. If you want the rock in the foreground with surfers and the peaks of Dois Irmãos behind the sunset, Pedra do Arpoador is the alternative viewpoint. It is busier, and the rock can be slippery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the sea to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out. As the light fades, try night mode and rest your elbows on the wall or rail to keep the phone steady. A Live Photo can catch the movement of waves and surfers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk suits this view, when the beach lights come on. The sun only sets over the sea from Arpoador around midsummer, and it is busy then, so arrive early to get a spot.

text.access_note: The park overlook is an open public space. The rock is also open to the public with walkways, but keep clear of the surf line.

name: Sambadrome Marquês de Sapucaí
label: Sambadrome
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça da Apoteose' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praça da Apoteose' (way/168385110): middle (193 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/34306743: large area 'Sambadrome Marquês de Sapucaí' (794 m across): the middle of the area.
notes: Carnival parade avenue.

text.description:
The Sambadrome is the purpose-built parade ground where Rio's samba schools compete during Carnival. Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and it was commissioned in 1983 and finished in 1984. The parade avenue is a 700 m stretch of Marquês de Sapucaí street with grandstands on both sides, and the whole venue holds about 90,000 people. At the far end is the Praça da Apoteose, where Niemeyer's 90 m trilegged concrete arch stands. It has become a symbol of the Carnival.

From the square you can stand by the arch and see the end of the avenue framed by the stands. The shapes are big, simple and repeated, so even a quick snap looks composed. Underneath the bleachers there is also a school with 115 classrooms, which tells you this is a working part of the city as well as a Carnival stage.

The parades take place over four nights just before Lent, starting at 8pm, so the grandstands are ticketed on those nights. Outside Carnival the square is sometimes used for concerts. The most reliable plan is a daytime visit to the square for the arch, with the stands behind you or to the side to add scale. If you want the wide view down the avenue, the grandstands are the place for it, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Sambadrome is in Cidade Nova, in downtown Rio de Janeiro. The Praça da Apoteose at its far end sits near the Morro da Mineira.
text.directions_text: Head for Cidade Nova in downtown Rio de Janeiro, which is the nearest well-known area. No stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so check a local map or transport app for the best way to reach the Sambódromo or Praça da Apoteose. From the square, the middle of the parade area is about 4 minutes on foot to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole arch and the stands into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the avenue's end. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the legs of the arch against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça da Apoteose (under the large concrete arch at the end of the avenue). The avenue's far end and the concrete arch that the parading schools pass under, framed by the sambódromo's stands. The avenue runs away from you to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the arch in the centre or on one third of the frame, with the stands forming the sides. Crouch a little and keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. For a different view, the grandstands give a wide panorama down the 700 m avenue. On parade nights the schools march from right to left toward the arch, so you can use panorama mode or the ultra-wide there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the arch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the concrete keeps its detail against a bright sky. On parade nights, use night mode only for the stands and avenue. For dancers and floats that move, a Live Photo or a quick burst of shots will work better.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the square can be visited, and aim for early morning or late afternoon, when the light on the concrete is softer. On parade nights, which start at 8pm just before Lent, the avenue is at its liveliest.

text.access_note: The square is an open-air space that a guide says visitors can enter by day, but the avenue and grandstands are ticketed on parade nights, so check the official site before you go.

name: Rio de Janeiro Cathedral
label: Metropolitan Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça da Cruz Vermelha' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praça da Cruz Vermelha' (way/1051466525): middle (86 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30621926: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rio de Janeiro Cathedral' (153 m across).
notes: Cone-shaped modernist cathedral with huge stained glass.

text.description:
Rio's cathedral looks nothing like a traditional church. It is a huge cone, designed by Edgar de Oliveira da Fonseca in a modern style inspired by Mayan pyramids. It was built between 1964 and 1979 and stands in the middle of the city. It is dedicated to Saint Sebastian, the patron saint of Rio de Janeiro.

The numbers help explain why it is hard to photograph up close. The cone is about 75 metres high and about 106 metres across on the outside. Four tall stained glass windows rise 64 metres inside, though this page is about the outside view. The open space of Praça da Cruz Vermelha gives you enough distance to see the whole cone and its exterior in one shot, which is why it is the standard outdoor view.

The simple, strong shape suits a phone. Put the cone in the frame with some sky around it, and the image reads clearly even on a small screen. Stay back rather than standing right at the walls, where the building fills the frame and the lines lean inwards. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the cone looks steady.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the centre of Rio de Janeiro.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot. From there the cathedral lies to the east, about 10 minutes on foot. Walk towards the cone, which is easy to spot from a distance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole cone. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter, cleaner shape. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and want to fit the full height in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça da Cruz Vermelha. The cathedral's cone and exterior from the open square, the standard outdoor view of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the cone up with the centre of the frame, with a little sky above it. Keep the phone upright and level so the sides don't lean. For a different view, try Largo da Lapa, where the Carioca Aqueduct arches sit in front of the cathedral, or Parque das Ruínas for a distant view over Lapa.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Take a few frames at different zoom levels and pick the best.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the building than the harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.
Standing right beside the cathedral walls makes the vertical lines lean inwards in a phone photo.
Largo da Lapa is in Lapa and Parque das Ruínas is in Santa Teresa, and the walk to them may involve some climbing.

name: Carioca Aqueduct
label: Arcos da Lapa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rua do Lavradio' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rua do Lavradio nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/154966398: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Arcos da Lapa' (310 m across).
notes: White colonial arches carrying the Santa Teresa tram.

text.description:
The Carioca Aqueduct, better known locally as Arcos da Lapa, is a long row of white stone arches that stands out against the rest of Lapa. It was inaugurated in 1750 to bring fresh water from the Carioca River into the city. The stretch between the Santa Teresa and Santo Antônio hills is about 270 metres long. It has two storeys of arches, 42 in total, up to 17.6 metres high. Since 1896 the top level has carried the little Santa Teresa tram, so you may catch the little Santa Teresa tram crossing the arches.

The arches photograph well because the repeating shapes make a strong pattern and the scale is easy to read. That angle gives depth, with the arches stepping away into the distance and everyday Lapa life in the foreground. Keep the whole structure in view if you can, and let a passer-by or a parked car add a sense of size.

If you would like the classic head-on view, walk to the open space below the arches. Rua Teotônio Regadas is another option, with colourful murals along the street.
text.geographic_location: The aqueduct is in the Lapa neighbourhood, in the centre of Rio de Janeiro, on the way up towards Santa Teresa. Rua do Lavradio is a street just south-west of the arches.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for the Lapa neighbourhood in the city centre and make your way on foot to Rua do Lavradio. Walk towards them and you will soon be underneath. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the long row of arches into the frame from the street. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. If you have a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the pattern of the upper arches or a tram crossing.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rua do Lavradio. A street-level view of the arches from a nearby street, framing the aqueduct at an angle rather than straight on. From here the arches sit to the north-east, seen at an angle along the street rather than straight on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the angle to your advantage: let the arches recede diagonally across the frame, with the street and a bit of Lapa life in the foreground. Turn on gridlines and line up the top of the arches with a horizontal line so they don't look tilted. For the classic head-on view, with the whole double row of arches, walk over to Arcos da Lapa itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the arches to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white stone keeps its detail and the sky does not look washed out. If a tram is crossing, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides advise going early or at dusk. The tram only crosses now and then, so check the timing if you want it in the picture. Avoid the area alone at night.

text.access_note: The arches can be seen from the open public street; the tram that crosses them is a separate service, so check the official site before you go for running times and ticket details.

name: Rodrigo de Freitas Lagoon
label: Rodrigo de Freitas
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque dos Patins' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque dos Patins' (way/462451555): edge nearest the subject (670 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2138398: large area 'Rodrigo de Freitas Lagoon' (2667 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Lagoon ringed by mountains and the Christ statue.

text.description:
Rodrigo de Freitas Lagoon (Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas in Portuguese) is a large lagoon in the middle of Rio's South Zone, ringed by hills, apartment blocks and a cycle path. It is sometimes called "the Heart of Rio de Janeiro". The water covers about 2.4 million square metres, and the paved path around it is about 7.5 kilometres long, so there are plenty of places to stop and look. It is linked to the Atlantic by the Jardim de Alah canal. The name comes from Rodrigo de Freitas de Carvalho, who married into the landowning Fagundes family in 1702. At Christmas a huge tree on a floating platform moves around the lagoon.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is from Parque dos Patins, a shaded park on the lakeside shore. Open water fills the foreground and the Corcovado massif rises behind it, which gives you a simple, layered picture of water, hill and sky. Food kiosks and paths are close by, so it is easy to pause and wait for the light. Keep the horizon level and put a strip of water, a strip of hill and a good slice of sky in the frame. If you are reasonably fit, Mirante do Sacopã is an alternative: a steep trail of about 15 to 20 minutes leads to a wide panorama over the whole lagoon, with the sea and the Ipanema and Leblon coast in the distance. Swimming in the lagoon is not recommended.
text.geographic_location: The lagoon lies in the district of Lagoa in Rio de Janeiro's Zona Sul (South Zone). It is surrounded by Ipanema, Leblon, Gávea, Jardim Botânico, Humaitá, Botafogo and Copacabana.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach Parque dos Patins on the lagoon shore. The lagoon lies about 432 m to the east of that point. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the water, the hill and a big sky together. The default lens (1x) gives a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Corcovado closer and make it feel larger behind the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque dos Patins (lakeside shore of the lagoon). Open water of the lagoon in the foreground with the Corcovado massif rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower or upper third line. Keep a little shoreline or a tree branch at the edge of the frame for depth. If you have time and are fit enough for the steep trail, Mirante do Sacopã is a second viewpoint, with a wider panorama of the whole lagoon and the coast beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the hill to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for the wide sweep of water, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset, when the sun goes down behind the hills and the light is softer. Midday light tends to look flat and hot.

text.access_note: Parque dos Patins is a lakeside park with paths and kiosks, but check the official site before you go in case of local changes or restrictions.

name: Fort Copacabana
label: Copacabana Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Forte de Copacabana' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Forte de Copacabana' (way/970021004): middle (530 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/371926003: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Forte de Copacabana' (133 m across).
notes: Historic fort at the end of Copacabana beach.

text.description: Fort Copacabana sits on the rocky point at the south end of Copacabana Beach, and it is one of the best places to see the whole bay in one frame. The army began building it in 1908 to guard the beach and the harbour entrance, and it was finished in 1914. Its two armoured gun turrets (cupolas) still stand. One held a pair of 305 mm guns and the other a pair of 190 mm guns. They are among the last heavy cupolas of their kind left in the world. In 1922 the fort was the centre of a short army revolt, and it was deactivated as a coastal artillery post in 1987. Today it also houses the Army Historical Museum, and it was a venue for the 2016 Olympics. For photographs, the upper parapet and gun-turret area is the draw. Looking north, you see the full curve of the beach running back towards Leme, with Sugarloaf Mountain behind it. Several guides call this the classic angle, because the point gives the longest view along the bay. The grey turrets and old walls also make a strong foreground. Bring photo ID, because the fort is a working army site. Allow time to stroll the museum's outdoor display of old artillery pieces, which also make good close-up subjects.
text.geographic_location: Fort Copacabana is at the southern end of Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro, on the headland at the south end of Copacabana Beach. It is next to the Copacabana district.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the south end of Copacabana Beach and ask for Forte de Copacabana. If you are already on the beach, walk along the beach promenade and Avenida Atlântica toward the fort at the south end of the beach. Allow extra time at the gate for the ID check. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the beach from the parapet. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the turrets and walls. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Sugarloaf Mountain closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (upper parapet and gun-turret area, looking north along the beach). The full curve of Copacabana Beach running back toward Leme, with Sugarloaf Mountain behind it. For an alternative, the approach along Avenida Atlântica shows the fort's walls with the sea on the other side of the path, but this is a weaker view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the beach along one of the lower lines, with Sugarloaf near the top third. Keep a piece of parapet or a turret in one corner of the frame to give depth. Try the same view in panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or the sky, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the beach does not wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few shots in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon for the light on Sugarloaf. Early morning, or a weekday opening, for fewer people.

text.access_note: The fort is a working army site with a museum and entry is charged, so check the official site for current prices and hours before you go, and bring photo ID.

name: Flamengo Park
label: Flamengo Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praia do Flamengo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praia do Flamengo' (relation/5548033): edge nearest the subject (1660 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1124430: large area 'Aterro do Flamengo' (3934 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Waterfront park with views of Sugarloaf.

text.description:
Flamengo Park, also called Aterro do Flamengo, is a long strip of green running beside Guanabara Bay. It is the largest public park in Rio de Janeiro, and it is described as the largest urban seaside park in the world. It covers about 120 hectares and was finished in 1965. Lota de Macedo Soares first imagined it, Affonso Eduardo Reidy designed it, and Roberto Burle Marx laid out the gardens. Inside you will find the Museum of Modern Art, the Carmen Miranda Museum and the World War II memorial.

For a phone photo, the best-known picture is taken from Praia do Flamengo, at the western end of the beach. From there Sugarloaf Mountain rises over the bay, with the sand and the palm-lined promenade in front of it. Guides often call this the classic Sugarloaf postcard angle, and it is an easy walk from the park. The wide open bay gives you plenty of sky and water, so the picture stays simple and uncluttered.

If you have time, two other places are worth a look: the concrete arches of the Monumento aos Pracinhas, and the Chinese-style gazebo at Vista Chinesa, which looks across the bay towards Sugarloaf. Keep your phone ready on the promenade, because joggers and cyclists pass often and make a lively foreground.
text.geographic_location: Flamengo Park runs along Guanabara Bay in the Flamengo district of Rio de Janeiro, between Downtown and Copacabana.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full postcard view of beach, promenade and Sugarloaf. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the promenade and palms in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Sugarloaf closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praia do Flamengo (western end of the beach). Sugarloaf Mountain rising over the bay, with the beach and palm-lined promenade in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line so the bay and the sky both get room. Place a few palms or the curve of the promenade along one edge to lead the eye towards Sugarloaf. For something different, the Monumento aos Pracinhas arches or the gazebo at Vista Chinesa make good alternative viewpoints.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on Sugarloaf to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Hold the phone steady and take a few frames, because walkers and cyclists often cross the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and crowds are thinner.

text.access_note: Flamengo Park is open public parkland and beach with no restrictions reported, but check the official site before you go in case of events or closures.

name: Paço Imperial
label: Paço Imperial
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça XV de Novembro' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praça Quinze de Novembro' (relation/7436360): middle (389 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4514671: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Paço Imperial' (123 m across).
notes: Former colonial royal palace on Praça XV.

text.description:
The Paço Imperial is one of Brazil's most important historic buildings, in the centre of Rio. It was finished in 1743 in a plain Baroque style as the home of the colonial governors. It later became the Viceroy's Palace, then a royal palace from 1808, and after 1822 the working palace of Brazil's emperors. On 9 January 1822 Pedro I announced from one of its balconies facing the square that he would stay in Brazil, and in 1888 Princess Isabel signed the Lei Áurea, which ended slavery, in one of its rooms. After a long spell as a post office, a major restoration in 1980 returned it to the look it had around 1818. Since 1984 it has been a cultural centre.

It photographs well because it faces Praça XV de Novembro, an open square. You can step back far enough to get the whole colonial-style front into one frame, with the General Osório monument and the surrounding Centro buildings close by. The long, simple facade, the rows of windows and the balconies give a clean, balanced picture. The Baroque doorway, made of Portuguese marble, is worth a closer shot.

Stand in front of the facade, facing the palace across the square. Early morning is the best time, when one guide describes the light as soft and warm on the building.
text.geographic_location: The Paço Imperial is in Centro, the historic heart of Rio de Janeiro. It sits on Praça XV de Novembro, facing the open square.
text.directions_text: Head for Praça XV de Novembro in Centro. From there it is about 2 minutes on foot to the palace itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the whole front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or the square is busy and the building will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the marble doorway, the balconies and the windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça XV de Novembro (front of the facade, facing the building across the square). The full colonial-style front of the palace framed by the open square, with the General Osório monument and the surrounding Centro buildings nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal line so the facade does not lean. Keep the building centred and leave a little square in the foreground. Hold the phone level, not tilted up, to keep the walls straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and detail. If people walk through the frame, take a few shots or try a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when one guide describes the light as soft and warm on the facade.

text.access_note: The square in front is open public space, but the palace and its cultural centre may have their own visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Theatro Municipal
label: Theatro Municipal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça Marechal Floriano' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Praça Floriano' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/107748847: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Theatro Municipal' (122 m across).
notes: Ornate opera house in the centre.

text.description:
The Theatro Municipal is Rio's opera house, and it is considered one of the most beautiful and important theatres in Brazil. It was modelled on the Paris Opéra of Charles Garnier, and the front is full of detail: a central sculptural group, and the names of classic European and Brazilian artists inscribed on the outer walls. Building began in 1905 on a foundation of 1,180 wood poles, and the theatre opened on 14 July 1909. Today it seats 2,361 and mostly stages ballet and classical music.

It photographs well because the main facade faces Cinelândia, the open square also called Praça Marechal Floriano. That gives you room to stand back and take in the whole front in one frame. The National Library and the National Fine Arts Museum are close by, so the surroundings add to the picture.

For the classic shot, stand across the square, in front of the main facade, and look towards the building. Keep your phone level so the columns don't lean, and try to keep passers-by out of the lower part of the frame, or let a few in for a sense of scale. If you have time, walk to the side streets for a different view. Avenida Rio Branco shows the flank and domes, and Avenida Treze de Maio gives a quieter angle on the facade and the sculpture on that side. The area is busy, so check conditions on the day.
text.geographic_location: In the Centro district of Rio de Janeiro, overlooking the Cinelândia square (Praça Marechal Floriano), close to the National Library and the National Fine Arts Museum.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. The spot is at Cinelândia in Centro. From there the theatre is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front and the open square into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the central sculptural group and the carved names on the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça Marechal Floriano (across the square, in front of the main facade). The full neoclassical front of the theatre with its central sculptural group, framed by the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean. Centre the sculptural group and leave a little space above the roof. For a different view, try Avenida Rio Branco for the side of the building and its domes, with the avenue leading towards it. Avenida Treze de Maio is quieter and shows the facade from the side, including the sculpture on that side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If you are there after dark and the building is lit, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day is kinder to the facade than harsh midday sun. Go when the square is quieter if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The square and the streets around the theatre are open public space; for the interior, guided tours are needed and flash is restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Candelária Church
label: Candelária Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça Pio X' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praça Pio X' (relation/5266298): middle (421 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30839484: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of Our Lady of the Candelária' (100 m across).
notes: Baroque and Renaissance church downtown.

text.description: Candelária Church is one of Rio's important historic churches, and its front is the part to photograph. The main facade was built between 1775 and 1811 in Portuguese colonial Baroque style, with some neoclassical touches such as the flat, two-dimensional front and the triangular pediment. Dark granite around the windows, doors and columns stands out against whitewashed wall, which gives the picture a clean, graphic look. The dome over the crossing was finished in 1877. It was made in white Lioz stone in Lisbon and shipped to Brazil, and when it was completed it was the tallest structure in the city. Both the bell towers and the dome can be seen from the open square in front, which is why that square is the usual base for the classic view. From there you can step well back and fit the whole facade into one frame, with the sky above and plenty of space around the building. For a different mood, Avenida Presidente Vargas offers a more urban picture, with the church set against modern skyscrapers and the straight lines of traffic. The church is also lit at night by a floodlighting scheme, so an evening visit can give you a second, quite different photo. Take a few wide shots first, then move closer for details of the towers and stonework.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Rio de Janeiro, facing the open square of Praça Pio X and close to Avenida Presidente Vargas.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot; head to Praça Pio X, the square in front of the church, in central Rio. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the square for the full facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the towers, dome and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça Pio X (in front of the church's main facade). The baroque-style front of the church framed by the open plaza, with the bell towers and dome visible.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Walk back across the plaza until the whole facade, the towers and the dome fit inside the frame. Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them so the building does not lean. For a more modern, contrasting picture, try the view from Avenida Presidente Vargas, where the church sits against skyscrapers and straight traffic lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the whitewash keeps its detail. Keep the phone level and avoid tilting it upwards, which makes the towers lean inward.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is best for the full facade. In the evening the church is lit by floodlights, so try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The square outside is open public space, but the church itself is a place of worship and may have set visiting times, so check the official site before you go.
